sections.title: A balanced diet supplies energy and building materials
paragraphs: A balanced diet supplies appropriate amounts of carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre. Balanced does not mean equal masses of every component. The required proportions depend on the person and their circumstances.

Starchy foods such as rice, bread and potatoes supply carbohydrate that can be digested to sugars used in respiration. Protein sources include beans, eggs, fish and meat; amino acids are used to make the body’s proteins for growth and repair. Proteins include enzymes, so their role is wider than simply making muscle.

Lipids from foods such as oils, nuts and dairy products supply an energy store and material for cell membranes. Stored fat also contributes to insulation and protection. Having a useful function does not mean that unlimited amounts are appropriate.

A meal containing carbohydrate and protein still needs evaluation of the other components and overall quantities. No single food has to supply every nutrient; the diet is considered across meals and time.

example.question: A menu contains only rice and oil. Why does including energy-rich food not make it a balanced diet?
steps: Carbohydrate and lipid can supply energy.
Check protein, required vitamins/minerals, water and fibre as well as total quantities.
A varied combination can supply components absent or inadequate in that menu.
example.explanation: Evaluate material and energy needs rather than counting equal portions.

practice.question: Does balanced mean seven equal portions by mass?
practice.answer: No. Appropriate amounts and proportions differ between components and people.
practice.explanation: Evaluate material and energy needs rather than counting equal portions.

commonMistakes: A nutrient’s useful role does not justify an unlimited amount.

sections.title: Connect vitamins A, C and D to their functions
paragraphs: Vitamin A supports normal vision, including seeing in low light. Eggs and dairy foods provide preformed vitamin A; orange or dark-green vegetables supply carotenoids that can be converted to vitamin A. These are source examples, not identical amounts in every food.

Vitamin C is needed for collagen formation and healthy connective tissues. Citrus fruits, peppers and other fruits and vegetables are sources. A serious shortage can lead to scurvy, involving weak connective tissues and poor healing.

Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and normal bone mineralisation. Oily fish, eggs and appropriately fortified foods are dietary examples; skin can also make vitamin D with suitable ultraviolet exposure. A severe shortage during growth can contribute to rickets.
Vitamins are needed in small quantities and do not supply food energy like carbohydrate or lipid. These roles explain syllabus examples; a symptom by itself is not a diagnosis of one deficiency.

example.question: Match a vitamin to vision, collagen formation and calcium absorption.
steps: A: normal vision.
C: collagen formation and connective-tissue maintenance.
D: calcium absorption supporting bones.
example.explanation: Pair each named vitamin with a specific function and a plausible dietary source.

practice.question: Would vitamin C replace carbohydrate as a respiration fuel?
practice.answer: No. Its essential role is different from supplying the main energy-rich substrates.
practice.explanation: Pair each named vitamin with a specific function and a plausible dietary source.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse vitamin D with the calcium mineral itself.

sections.title: Calcium, iron, water and fibre have different roles
paragraphs: Calcium contributes to bones and teeth and has other roles in cells. Dairy foods, calcium-fortified alternatives and some green vegetables are sources. Iron is part of haemoglobin, helping red blood cells transport oxygen; meat and pulses are examples of sources.

Insufficient iron can contribute to iron-deficiency anaemia and reduced oxygen transport. Anaemia can have other causes, so neither tiredness nor a low haemoglobin result automatically establishes the dietary cause.

Water is a solvent and transport medium for many substances and provides a medium for cellular reactions. Drinks and water-containing foods contribute to intake. Water does not have to be digested into smaller molecules before absorption.

Dietary fibre includes plant material such as cellulose that human digestive enzymes do not digest. Wholegrain foods, vegetables and pulses provide fibre; it contributes to the bulk and movement of gut contents. Fibre is not an enzyme and is not chemically identical to every carbohydrate in a meal.

example.question: Why do calcium, iron and fibre not have interchangeable functions?
steps: Calcium contributes to bones and teeth.
Iron is needed for haemoglobin and oxygen transport.
Fibre contributes to gut-content bulk and movement, rather than haemoglobin formation.
example.explanation: State a named component’s role instead of calling every component a source of energy.

practice.question: Can water be absorbed only after enzymatic digestion?
practice.answer: No. Water is already a small molecule and does not require that breakdown.
practice.explanation: State a named component’s role instead of calling every component a source of energy.

commonMistakes: Dietary fibre and soluble digested sugars are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Activity, growth and pregnancy affect requirements
paragraphs: The body transfers energy in respiration for muscle activity, temperature regulation and other cell processes. A person doing more muscular activity generally needs more energy than the same person at rest, all else equal.

Age affects requirements through growth, body size and activity. A growing child needs material and energy for new tissue, but this does not mean every child has a larger total energy requirement than every adult. An adult’s larger body can require more energy overall.

Pregnancy involves developing fetal and maternal tissues and changes in physiological demand. Requirements can rise, but the amount varies with stage and circumstances; “eat twice as much” is not a valid biological deduction.

For an exam comparison, use the factors stated in the question. The site does not assign personal daily calorie targets from age alone. Energy needs and needs for particular nutrients are connected but are not the same quantity.

example.question: Two otherwise similar people differ only in daily physical activity. Explain the expected energy-demand difference.
steps: The more active person’s muscles carry out more work.
Respiration supplies the additional energy transfers for contraction.
Other differences such as body size would need consideration if not controlled.
example.explanation: Compare the stated conditions and qualify variables that have not been controlled.

practice.question: Must a young child need more total energy than a large active adult?
practice.answer: No. Growth matters, but body size and activity also affect the total.
practice.explanation: Compare the stated conditions and qualify variables that have not been controlled.

commonMistakes: A factor-based explanation is stronger than a universal age ranking.

sections.title: Follow food through the alimentary canal
paragraphs: The alimentary canal is the continuous route from mouth to anus. In the mouth, chewing breaks food into smaller pieces and saliva moistens it and supplies amylase. Swallowed food passes through the oesophagus towards the stomach.

The stomach stores and mixes food, secretes acid and begins protein digestion with proteases. Its lining is protected by mucus. Food then enters the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, receiving pancreatic secretions and bile.

The ileum is the later part of the small intestine. Digestion continues and the small intestine is the major site of absorption of digested nutrients. The pancreas is an accessory organ: it secretes digestive enzymes into the duodenum through a duct. Food does not pass through the pancreas.

The colon absorbs remaining water and salts from gut contents, and the rectum stores faeces before egestion through the anus. Much water has already been absorbed in the small intestine; the colon is not the only place water is absorbed. Egestion removes undigested material, whereas excretion removes metabolic waste.

example.question: Put mouth, stomach, ileum, colon and oesophagus in food-route order. Where does the pancreas fit?
steps: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon → rectum → anus.
The pancreas supplies secretions to the duodenum through a duct.
It is not a stage through which the swallowed food travels.
example.explanation: Separate the tube carrying food from organs delivering secretions to it.

practice.question: Is egestion of faeces the same process as excretion of urea?
practice.answer: No. Egestion removes undigested gut material; urea is metabolic waste removed by excretion.
practice.explanation: Separate the tube carrying food from organs delivering secretions to it.

commonMistakes: Do not put the pancreas, liver or gall bladder into the food passage route.

sections.title: Muscle waves move food along the gut
paragraphs: Peristalsis is coordinated contraction and relaxation of muscles in the gut wall that moves contents along. A bolus is a mass of swallowed food. Circular muscle contracts behind it, narrowing the lumen and helping push it towards a region that can receive it.
Longitudinal muscle changes the local length of the gut; coordinated muscle activity produces a moving wave. The process is active muscular movement, rather than food simply falling under gravity.

A useful drawing shows the lumen narrower behind the bolus and arrows along the food route. The wave travels; the entire gut does not remain tightly closed. Mixing movements also occur in the digestive tract, so not every contraction represents only forward transport.

example.question: Why can swallowed food move along the oesophagus when a person is not upright?
steps: Gut-wall muscles contract and relax in a coordinated wave.
Constriction behind the bolus helps push it along.
Gravity is not the only driving mechanism.
example.explanation: Describe the changing muscle pattern and connect it to movement of the contents.

practice.question: Would permanent contraction all along the gut provide effective onward movement?
practice.answer: No. Movement requires coordinated changes that leave a receiving region ahead.
practice.explanation: Describe the changing muscle pattern and connect it to movement of the contents.

commonMistakes: Peristalsis is not diffusion through a membrane.

sections.title: Starch digestion needs amylase and maltase
paragraphs: Amylase catalyses the breakdown of starch into smaller sugars, represented here by maltose. Salivary amylase acts in the mouth, and pancreatic amylase acts in the small intestine. It is inaccurate to attribute the whole starch-to-glucose sequence to amylase alone.

Maltase associated with the small-intestinal lining breaks maltose into glucose. The teaching sequence is starch → maltose → glucose, with the enzymes labelled above their respective steps. The enzyme itself is not a food-digestion product.

Digestion is chemical breakdown of larger molecules; absorption is movement of products through the gut lining. Glucose can be absorbed and transported to cells, then used in respiration or other processes. Making glucose available is not the same step as oxidising it in respiration.

example.question: Label both enzyme steps in starch → maltose → glucose.
steps: Amylase catalyses starch breakdown to maltose in the simplified sequence.
Maltase catalyses maltose breakdown to glucose.
Absorption occurs after suitable small products become available.
example.explanation: Keep substrate, enzyme, product and subsequent absorption separate.

practice.question: Is amylase the enzyme that specifically splits maltose to glucose?
practice.answer: No. That named step is catalysed by maltase.
practice.explanation: Keep substrate, enzyme, product and subsequent absorption separate.

commonMistakes: Name both enzymes when explaining the full specified starch-to-glucose route.

sections.title: Protein and lipid digestion yield different products
paragraphs: Proteases catalyse the breakdown of proteins into smaller peptides and, through further enzyme action, amino acids. Protein digestion begins in the stomach and continues in the small intestine. The overall syllabus product is amino acids; it is not glucose.

Lipases catalyse lipid digestion. The school summary represents lipids being broken into fatty acids and glycerol. In the body, digestion of triglycerides also forms intermediates such as monoglycerides, so the summary is an endpoint model rather than every single reaction step.

Enzymes have suitable pH and temperature conditions. Stomach acid supports stomach-protease action, while the small intestine provides different conditions for pancreatic and intestinal enzymes. Acid is not itself the named enzyme that hydrolyses protein.
Chewing and fat emulsification can provide more accessible surface for enzymes without being the same chemical process as enzyme-catalysed digestion.

example.question: A response says “lipase changes protein into glucose”. Correct its substrate and products.
steps: Lipase acts on lipids, not proteins.
Use fatty acids and glycerol for the specified overall lipid products.
Proteases instead contribute to proteins becoming amino acids.
example.explanation: Match each enzyme type to the correct food category and overall products.

practice.question: Is stomach hydrochloric acid a protease?
practice.answer: No. It provides acidic conditions; proteases are enzyme molecules catalysing protein breakdown.
practice.explanation: Match each enzyme type to the correct food category and overall products.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse the conditions supporting an enzyme with the enzyme itself.

sections.title: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder
paragraphs: The liver produces bile and the gall bladder stores and concentrates it. Bile passes through ducts into the duodenum. Neither organ is part of the route through which swallowed food directly passes.

Bile contributes to neutralising acidic contents arriving from the stomach, providing suitable less-acidic conditions in the small intestine. Pancreatic bicarbonate also contributes; bile is not the sole secretion involved in neutralisation.

Bile salts emulsify lipids, dispersing a large lipid mass into smaller droplets. This increases the surface area available to lipase. Emulsification is a physical change and does not by itself break lipid molecules into fatty acids and glycerol.
Bile is not a digestive enzyme. Keep its production, storage, delivery and two specified roles distinct. A small droplet has the same lipid molecules as before until chemical digestion occurs.

example.question: Explain how bile helps lipase without saying bile is lipase.
steps: Bile disperses lipid into smaller droplets.
The droplets provide more lipid surface for lipase action.
Lipase performs the chemical breakdown; emulsification does not.
example.explanation: Separate secretion location, physical dispersion and enzyme action.

practice.question: Which organ makes bile and which stores it?
practice.answer: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder stores and concentrates it.
practice.explanation: Separate secretion location, physical dispersion and enzyme action.

commonMistakes: Emulsification changes droplet size, not lipid molecules into digestive products.

sections.title: A villus provides a large area and short transfer distance
paragraphs: The small intestine has a large absorptive area from its length, folds, villi and microvilli on absorptive cells. A villus is a projection of the lining; microvilli are much smaller projections on individual cells. Neither term means an enzyme.

The epithelium is one cell thick, giving a short path between the gut lumen and the tissues below. A capillary network receives glucose and amino acids and carries them away, helping maintain conditions for continued absorption.

A central lacteal is a lymph vessel. Many absorbed long-chain lipid products are repackaged in the lining cells and enter the lymph through lacteals; not all digestion products enter the same vessel or use an identical membrane mechanism.

Absorption involves membrane transport, including carrier-mediated and energy-dependent steps as well as diffusion. A thin surface alone does not mean that every nutrient simply diffuses into blood. Relate area, distance and removal of absorbed material to the rate.

example.question: Explain two features of a villus that aid absorption.
steps: Large surface area gives more available membrane for transfer.
One-cell-thick epithelium provides a short transfer distance.
Capillaries carry away absorbed glucose and amino acids; a lacteal provides a lipid-transport route.
example.explanation: Link each named structure to area, distance or onward transport.

practice.question: Are a villus and a microvillus the same sized structure?
practice.answer: No. A villus contains many cells; microvilli are small projections on cell surfaces.
practice.explanation: Link each named structure to area, distance or onward transport.

commonMistakes: Do not claim every absorbed nutrient passes directly into a blood capillary by simple diffusion.

diagram.alt: Original schematic of one villus showing a one-cell-thick epithelium, surface microvilli, a blood-capillary loop and central lymph lacteal. Glucose and amino-acid transport is distinguished from the main long-chain lipid route. Not to scale; no universal simple-diffusion mechanism is implied.
diagram.caption: An original functional villus model. The capillary and lacteal are different routes; microvilli are projections on lining cells. Enlarged and not to scale.

sections.title: Paper 2B: estimate energy transferred from burning food
paragraphs: A school calorimetry model burns an approved food sample beneath a measured mass of water and records the water’s temperature increase. Compare the food’s mass before and after burning, using the mass actually burned as the denominator.

Using the supplied water heat-capacity value 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, the water’s energy increase is Q = mass of water × 4.2 × temperature rise. Divide by the mass of food burned to estimate energy transferred to the water per gram of food.

For illustrative inputs, 20.0 g of water rises from 21.0 °C to 31.0 °C while food mass falls from 1.20 g to 0.90 g. The temperature rise is 10.0 °C; water gains 840 J. Dividing by 0.30 g gives 2800 J g⁻¹, or 2.8 kJ g⁻¹.
The result estimates heat collected by the water in this setup. It is not a measured result from this project, nor the exact chemical energy of the food or energy absorbed by a human body.

example.question: Calculate the water-energy increase and energy per gram for the stated illustrative trial.
steps: Mass burned = 1.20 − 0.90 = 0.30 g.
Temperature rise = 31.0 − 21.0 = 10.0 °C.
example.explanation: Define the measured changes before substituting and convert joules to kilojoules explicitly.

practice.question: Would dividing by the whole 1.20 g initial food mass give the same intended estimate?
practice.answer: No. The specified method uses the 0.30 g mass burned, not the entire starting mass.
practice.explanation: Define the measured changes before substituting and convert joules to kilojoules explicitly.

commonMistakes: Use temperature change and mass lost; do not use final temperature or starting food mass.

apparatus: Teacher-approved food sample,holder and ignition equipment
Measured water in a suitable calorimetry container,thermometer and stirrer
Balance,heatproof surface and teacher-approved safety arrangement
method: Record the food/holder mass and measured water mass before heating.
Record initial water temperature and burn the approved sample at a controlled distance.
Stir gently and record final temperature; allow apparatus to cool safely before final mass measurement.
Calculate mass burned,temperature rise,water energy increase and energy per gram; repeat comparable trials.
variables: Compare approved food types; measure water temperature increase per gram burned.
Keep water mass,container,distance and starting conditions comparable.
safety: Teacher manages flame and hot apparatus; use eye protection and a heatproof surface.
Check food allergies and do not eat experimental samples; keep flammable materials clear.
quality: Record actual observations and residual burning conditions; these notes contain illustrative numbers only.
Heat losses,incomplete combustion and container heating limit the energy estimate.

sections.title: Paper 2B: evaluate heat losses and fair comparison
paragraphs: Energy can heat the air and apparatus instead of the water. Incomplete burning leaves chemical energy in residues. The collected-water estimate therefore commonly underestimates the food’s combustion energy.

For food comparisons, control water mass, apparatus, flame-to-container distance and starting conditions. Stir gently before reading so the temperature represents the water more fairly. Repeat and examine variation; one reading is weak evidence for a ranking.

The teacher selects the food and approved arrangement, checks allergies and manages ignition and hot apparatus. Do not eat experimental food. Use eye protection, a heatproof surface and safe handling of hot containers; a shield must not create an unsafe enclosed flame.

Insulation and suitable shielding can reduce losses, but claiming “no heat loss” after improvement is unjustified. A food-label value may be given per 100 g and may represent metabolically available energy; compare both basis and method before blaming a numerical difference on arithmetic.

example.question: Why might repeated open-flame calorimetry estimates be consistent but below a label value?
steps: Consistent heat loss can create a systematic underestimate.
Repeating improves evidence about spread, but does not eliminate that bias.
Check whether label and experimental values use the same energy definition and mass basis.
example.explanation: Distinguish improved repeatability from removal of a known loss mechanism.

practice.question: Does repeating the same leaky setup remove systematic heat loss?
practice.answer: No. It can show repeatability while the underestimate remains.
practice.explanation: Distinguish improved repeatability from removal of a known loss mechanism.

commonMistakes: Repeating alone does not eliminate a systematic bias.

sections.title: Evaluate a varied diet by component and function
paragraphs: A balanced diet supplies appropriate amounts of seven categories: carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre. The named vitamins and minerals are different members of those categories, not extra equal-sized portions. Evaluate the diet over time, using stated amounts and circumstances; a food name alone does not prove an adequate intake.

For a source–function chain, rice supplies starch for respiration fuel; beans or eggs supply protein for growth and repair; oil or nuts supply lipid for energy storage and membrane material. These foods can supply more than one component. A source example is not a claim that every serving has identical composition.

Carrot carotenoids can supply vitamin A precursors for normal vision; peppers supply vitamin C for collagen formation; oily fish or appropriately fortified foods supply vitamin D supporting calcium absorption and bones. Dairy foods or calcium-fortified alternatives supply calcium for bones and teeth. Pulses or meat supply iron for haemoglobin and oxygen transport. Vitamin D is not calcium, and none of these vitamins replaces an energy-rich fuel.

Drinks and water-containing foods supply water as a solvent and transport medium. Wholegrain foods, vegetables and pulses supply fibre that contributes to bulk and movement of gut contents. Human enzymes do not digest cellulose to glucose. No personal dosage, calorie target or deficiency diagnosis is inferred from these examples.

example.question: A fictional diet includes only white rice and oil. A student calls it balanced because it contains energy. Evaluate the claim.
steps: Rice and oil can provide carbohydrate and lipid, but energy alone does not cover material and regulatory requirements.
Check protein, vitamins, minerals, water and fibre and the amounts supplied across the diet. Adding a named food does not prove that its quantity is sufficient.
Appropriate proportions depend on context; seven equal masses are not the definition of balance.
example.explanation: Appropriate proportions depend on context; seven equal masses are not the definition of balance.

practice.question: For each source, identify the named component and one role: rice; eggs (protein); oil; carrots (carotenoids); peppers; oily fish (vitamin); calcium-fortified drink (mineral); pulses (iron); drinking water; wholegrain fibre. Then explain why seven equal masses and one varied meal do not prove a balanced long-term diet.
practice.answer: Rice: carbohydrate, respiration fuel. Eggs: protein, growth/repair. Oil: lipid, energy store or membranes. Carrots: vitamin A precursor, vision. Peppers: vitamin C, collagen. Oily fish: vitamin D, calcium absorption/bones. Fortified drink: calcium, bones/teeth. Iron in pulses: haemoglobin/oxygen transport. Water: solvent/transport. Fibre: gut-content bulk/movement. Required amounts differ and the diet must be considered over time; names alone do not establish adequacy.
practice.explanation: Appropriate proportions depend on context; seven equal masses are not the definition of balance.

commonMistakes: Do not count vitamin A, C and D as three equal meal portions or diagnose a deficiency from a menu alone.

sections.title: Explain energy requirements using the stated comparison
paragraphs: In a controlled comparison of the same person on two otherwise similar days, greater muscular activity increases energy transfers for contraction. Food substrates support respiration; the explanation links the activity to its demand rather than assigning an arbitrary daily intake.

Growth needs material and energy for making tissues. Age also changes body size and typical activity. A growing child can have high needs relative to body size without exceeding every large active adult in total energy requirement.

Pregnancy can increase demand as fetal and maternal tissues develop. Stage, size and activity still matter; pregnancy does not justify a universal instruction to double food intake. These are classroom comparisons, not personal nutritional prescriptions.

example.question: A person spends one otherwise similar day resting and another doing prolonged physical work. Predict the direction of change and identify a missing control.
steps: More muscular work needs additional energy transfers for contraction, supplied by respiration.
Expected energy requirement increases if other conditions stay comparable.
Body size, temperature and other activity must not be silently changed in the comparison.
example.explanation: Body size, temperature and other activity must not be silently changed in the comparison.

practice.question: Explain (a) why an otherwise similar more active person generally requires more energy, (b) why growth matters but cannot rank every child above every adult, and (c) why pregnancy may raise requirements without implying twice as much food.
practice.answer: Activity increases muscular energy demand. Growth requires tissue material and energy, while total demand also depends on body size/activity. Developing fetal and maternal tissues can raise pregnancy requirements, but stage and circumstances vary; doubling intake does not follow.
practice.explanation: Body size, temperature and other activity must not be silently changed in the comparison.

commonMistakes: Age is a contributing factor, not a universal ranking of total energy needs.

sections.title: Separate the food route from secretion routes
paragraphs: The original diagram is a functional route map, not an anatomical position drawing. Solid crimson arrows follow swallowed material. Dashed amber arrows represent secretions from accessory organs. Food passes through A mouth, B oesophagus, C stomach, D duodenum, E ileum, F colon, G rectum and then the anus. The jejunum and some other details are omitted for this specified route; the two small-intestine boxes are not adjacent measured lengths.

A mouth chews, mixes with saliva and begins starch digestion. B oesophagus transports a bolus by peristalsis. C stomach mixes and stores contents, provides acid and supports protease action. D duodenum receives bile and pancreatic enzymes; E ileum participates in continuing digestion and absorption. F colon absorbs remaining water/salts; G rectum stores faeces before egestion.

H pancreas delivers digestive enzymes into the duodenum through a duct; it is not a food passage. I liver makes bile and J gall bladder stores and concentrates it before release to the duodenum. Storage is not production. A blocked secretion duct can impair delivery while leaving a route for food through the gut.

Peristalsis uses coordinated contraction and relaxation in the gut wall. Constriction behind a bolus and a receiving region ahead help move contents forward. The wave moves rather than the entire tube remaining shut, and transport does not rely solely on gravity.

example.question: The duct from H to D is blocked in a fictional model, while the gut tube is open. Does swallowed food now pass through H?
steps: No: H is the pancreas, an accessory organ that supplies secretions.
Food still follows the solid-arrow route through D; enzyme delivery from H is reduced in this simplified model.
A secretion-route change must not be turned into a new food-route stage.
example.explanation: A secretion-route change must not be turned into a new food-route stage.

practice.question: Use A–J to trace swallowed food from mouth to exit and give the function of A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H. Identify where bile is made and stored. Explain why a bolus can be transported along a horizontal oesophagus and why permanent contraction of the whole tube would fail.
practice.answer: Food: A→B→C→D→E→F→G→anus (intermediate details omitted). A chews/mixes saliva; B transports by peristalsis; C mixes/stores and supplies acid/proteases; D receives bile/pancreatic enzymes; E digests/absorbs nutrients; F absorbs remaining water/salts; G stores faeces; H supplies digestive enzymes to D. I makes bile; J stores it. Coordinated constriction behind and relaxation ahead move a bolus without depending on gravity; permanent whole-tube contraction removes the receiving region.
practice.explanation: A secretion-route change must not be turned into a new food-route stage.

commonMistakes: The diagram is a route abstraction, not a measurement or a full anatomical drawing.

diagram.alt: Original functional flow map. A mouth, B oesophagus, C stomach, D duodenum, E ileum, F colon and G rectum form the food route to the anus. H pancreas sends secretions to D; I liver supplies bile through J gall bladder to D. Crimson solid and amber dashed arrows distinguish routes; not anatomical or to scale.
diagram.caption: Follow solid arrows for food; follow dashed arrows for secretions. Original simplified route map: positions, lengths and omitted gut details are not anatomical measurements.

sections.title: Use substrate changes to distinguish digestion and emulsification
paragraphs: In the simplified starch sequence, amylase catalyses starch to maltose and maltase catalyses maltose to glucose. Amylase and maltase are not interchangeable. Proteases contribute to protein breakdown to amino acids; lipases contribute to lipid breakdown with fatty acids and glycerol as the specified overall products.

Chemical digestion changes large food molecules into smaller products. Chewing and emulsification increase accessible surface without themselves producing those chemical products. Bile salts break a large lipid mass into smaller droplets; lipase acts on the lipid molecules.

Bile contributes to neutralising acidic stomach contents in the small intestine, alongside other secretions such as pancreatic bicarbonate. Suitable conditions support enzymes; neutralisation is not itself enzyme-catalysed food breakdown. These roles explain why a larger lipid surface can aid lipase without making bile a lipase.

example.question: A model produces smaller lipid droplets after bile is added but detects no fatty-acid increase. Has it demonstrated lipase digestion?
steps: The smaller droplets support physical emulsification in this model.
No product evidence is supplied for lipid hydrolysis; emulsification alone does not produce fatty acids/glycerol.
Lipase and suitable conditions are needed for the specified chemical breakdown.
example.explanation: Lipase and suitable conditions are needed for the specified chemical breakdown.

practice.question: Correct these claims: amylase alone converts starch through maltose to glucose; protease produces glucose from protein; lipase produces amino acids; bile is the enzyme that splits lipids. Then explain the two ways bile helps small-intestinal digestion.
practice.answer: Amylase: starch→maltose; maltase: maltose→glucose. Proteases: protein→amino acids overall. Lipases: lipids→fatty acids and glycerol overall. Bile is not an enzyme: it contributes to neutralising acid and emulsifies lipid into smaller droplets, increasing surface available to lipase without chemically splitting lipid molecules.
practice.explanation: Lipase and suitable conditions are needed for the specified chemical breakdown.

commonMistakes: A physical droplet change does not by itself prove chemical digestion.

sections.title: Predict absorption changes from a villus feature
paragraphs: Compare a villus with a hypothetical smooth surface of the same outer dimensions. Folds, villi and cell-surface microvilli provide more available absorptive area. A one-cell-thick epithelium gives a short crossing path; neither feature creates digestive enzymes by itself.

Capillaries carry away absorbed glucose and amino acids. This removal supports continuing transfer rather than allowing absorbed products simply to accumulate next to the lining. A lacteal is a separate lymph vessel that receives many repackaged long-chain lipid products.

The earlier original villus diagram shows these separate structures. It is a schematic, not microscopy. Nutrients can cross by different membrane transport mechanisms; a short path does not imply universal simple diffusion or a single destination vessel.

example.question: In a fictional comparison, lining cells lose many microvilli while the intestine length and wall thickness stay the same. Identify the direct structural disadvantage.
steps: Absorptive area falls even though the specified length and thickness are unchanged.
Less membrane is available for transfer under otherwise comparable conditions.
This does not show that all transport mechanisms or vessels have disappeared.
example.explanation: This does not show that all transport mechanisms or vessels have disappeared.

practice.question: Explain why (a) fewer microvilli, (b) a thicker epithelial layer and (c) slower capillary removal can impair absorption. Identify the main onward route for many absorbed long-chain lipid products, and distinguish villi from microvilli.
practice.answer: Fewer microvilli reduce area; a thicker lining lengthens the crossing path; slower blood removal reduces onward transport and can reduce conditions supporting continued transfer. Many repackaged long-chain lipid products enter lacteals/lymph. A villus contains many cells; microvilli are much smaller projections on individual lining cells. Different products do not all cross by simple diffusion or enter the same vessel.
practice.explanation: This does not show that all transport mechanisms or vessels have disappeared.

commonMistakes: Explain the stated changed feature rather than claiming an unmeasured change in all absorption processes.

sections.title: Paper 2B: compare collected heat per gram burned
paragraphs: The table contains invented classroom readings, not trials performed by this project. Use change in water temperature and the food mass actually burned, with supplied specific heat capacity 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹: Q = water mass × 4.2 × temperature rise. Divide Q by burned mass, then divide by 1000 for kJ g⁻¹.

A higher temperature rise alone does not establish more energy per gram: water mass and mass burned can differ. Trial P gives 2520 J/0.40 g = 6.30 kJ g⁻¹; Q gives 3528 J/0.70 g = 5.04 kJ g⁻¹; R gives 1890 J/0.30 g = 6.30 kJ g⁻¹. These are collected-water estimates, not exact combustion energies or human dietary intake values.

Keep water mass, container, flame-to-container distance and starting conditions comparable when investigating food type. Repeat to examine variation, but a repeatable open setup can still lose heat systematically. Container heating, heat loss and incomplete burning limit the inference; do not rank true food energy from these single unequal trials.

The teacher selects an approved non-nut food and checks allergies, manages ignition and hot apparatus, and uses eye protection and a heatproof surface. Do not eat experimental samples. Cool safely before reweighing. Shielding or insulation must not create an unsafe enclosed flame; improvements reduce losses without proving zero loss. This describes supervised practical design, not an instruction to perform it alone.

example.question: An independent illustrative setup heats 40.0 g water from 19.0 to 26.5 °C while food mass falls from 1.10 to 0.85 g. Calculate collected energy per gram burned.
steps: Temperature rise = 7.5 °C; food burned = 0.25 g.
The denominator is mass burned; neither final temperature nor initial food mass substitutes for a change.
example.explanation: The denominator is mass burned; neither final temperature nor initial food mass substitutes for a change.

practice.question: From P, Q and R, calculate mass burned, temperature rise, Q and kJ per gram. Explain why R’s highest temperature rise does not prove the highest true food energy. Name two controlled variables, one systematic limitation, the role of repeats and two safety measures.
practice.answer: P: 0.40 g, 6.0 °C, 2520 J, 6.30 kJ g⁻¹. Q: 0.70 g, 8.4 °C, 3528 J, 5.04 kJ g⁻¹. R: 0.30 g, 9.0 °C, 1890 J, 6.30 kJ g⁻¹. Water mass and mass burned differ; R and P have equal collected energy per gram. Single biased readings do not rank true food energy. Control water mass/container/distance/start conditions; heat loss can systematically lower estimates. Repeats show spread but do not remove that bias. Teacher-managed flame/hot apparatus, eye protection, heatproof surface, allergy checks/non-nut food and no eating are acceptable safety points.
practice.explanation: The denominator is mass burned; neither final temperature nor initial food mass substitutes for a change.

commonMistakes: Do not rank food energy using only the largest temperature rise or pretend invented readings are observed trials.
